# Introduction

**Objective.** Discover which products customers of a UK online gift retailer buy
*together*, and convert those co-occurrence patterns into actionable
merchandising rules.

**Dataset.** UCI Machine Learning Repository #352, *Online Retail* — every
transaction of a UK-based, registered, non-store online retailer between
**1 December 2010 and 9 December 2011**. The company mainly sells unique
all-occasion giftware; many customers are wholesalers.

| Attribute | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `InvoiceNo`   | Transaction ID. A leading `C` marks a cancellation. |
| `StockCode`   | Product code. |
| `Description` | Product name. |
| `Quantity`    | Units of the product on that invoice line. |
| `InvoiceDate` | Timestamp of the transaction. |
| `UnitPrice`   | Unit price in GBP. |
| `CustomerID`  | Customer number (often missing). |
| `Country`     | Country of the customer. |

**Method.** The Apriori algorithm (Agrawal & Srikant, 1994) as implemented in the
R package `arules`, with rule visualisation from `arulesViz`.

## The three measures

For an association rule $X \Rightarrow Y$ over a set of $N$ transactions:

$$
\text{support}(X \Rightarrow Y) = P(X \cup Y) = \frac{|\{t : X \cup Y \subseteq t\}|}{N}
$$

$$
\text{confidence}(X \Rightarrow Y) = P(Y \mid X) = \frac{\text{support}(X \cup Y)}{\text{support}(X)}
$$

$$
\text{lift}(X \Rightarrow Y) = \frac{\text{confidence}(X \Rightarrow Y)}{\text{support}(Y)} = \frac{P(X \cup Y)}{P(X)P(Y)}
$$

* **Support** — how common the pattern is. Governs whether a rule is worth acting on at all.
* **Confidence** — how reliable it is. High confidence alone is misleading when $Y$ is a bestseller bought by nearly everyone.
* **Lift** — how much better than chance. $\text{lift} = 1$ means independence, $> 1$ means the products genuinely attract each other, $< 1$ means they repel.

**The Apriori property**, which makes the search tractable: *every subset of a
frequent itemset is itself frequent*. Equivalently, if an itemset is
infrequent, every superset of it is infrequent too and can be pruned without
being counted. Without this, mining `r format(ncol(trans), big.mark = ",")`
distinct products would mean evaluating $2^{`r ncol(trans)`}$ candidate itemsets.

---

# Data preparation

## Quality audit of the raw file

```{r audit}
knitr::kable(tab("01_data_quality_audit"), format.args = list(big.mark = ","))
```

Four problems had to be resolved before mining:

1. **Cancellations** (`InvoiceNo` starting with `C`) and **negative quantities**
   are returns, not purchases. Leaving them in would fabricate co-occurrences
   that never happened.
2. **Zero or negative unit prices** are adjustments and free samples.
3. **Non-product stock codes** (`POST`, `DOT`, `M`, `BANK CHARGES`,
   `AMAZONFEE`, …) are postage and administrative lines. They appear on a huge
   share of invoices, so they would dominate every rule while carrying no
   merchandising meaning.
4. **Free-text junk descriptions** ("damaged", "check", "?", "found", "lost") are
   warehouse notes, not products.

Additionally, each `StockCode` was pinned to a single canonical description
(descriptions drift across rows for the same product), duplicate item lines
within an invoice were collapsed, and **single-item baskets were dropped** —
a basket of one contains no co-occurrence information and only dilutes support.

## Result

```{r cleaning}
knitr::kable(tab("01_cleaning_summary"))
```

# Exploratory analysis

## What sells most often

```{r fig-items}
fig("01_top_items_frequency")
```

```{r fig-revenue}
fig("02_top_items_revenue")
```

Frequency and revenue rank products very differently. `WHITE HANGING HEART
T-LIGHT HOLDER` leads on basket count, but high-ticket items such as
`REGENCY CAKESTAND 3 TIER` and `PAPER CRAFT , LITTLE BIRDIE` climb the revenue
table. Market basket analysis works on the *frequency* view — which is why a
rule with a modest support figure can still be commercially significant.

## Basket size

```{r fig-basket}
fig("03_basket_size_distribution")
```

```{r basket-stats}
knitr::kable(tab("02_basket_size_stats"))
```

The distribution is heavily right-skewed. The long tail is the wholesale
customers — baskets of a hundred or more distinct products. These large baskets
generate an enormous number of item pairs and are the main reason support values
in this dataset stay low even for strong rules.

## Time and geography

```{r fig-month}
fig("04_monthly_revenue")
```

```{r fig-heat}
fig("05_weekday_hour_heatmap")
```

```{r fig-country}
fig("06_top_countries")
```

Three operational facts fall out: revenue peaks sharply in the pre-Christmas
quarter (September–November), trading is concentrated on weekday business hours
with essentially no Saturday activity, and the UK dominates revenue while the
Netherlands, Ireland and Germany form a meaningful second tier.

# Association rules

## Parameters and the pipeline of filters

```{r params}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Parameter = c("Minimum support", "Minimum confidence", "Rule length",
                "Minimum lift", "Significance test"),
  Value = c(paste0(PARAMS$support * 100, "% (about ",
                   round(PARAMS$support * length(trans)), " baskets)"),
            paste0(PARAMS$confidence * 100, "%"),
            paste(PARAMS$minlen, "to", PARAMS$maxlen, "items"),
            paste(">", PARAMS$min_lift),
            "Fisher's exact test, Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted, p < 0.05")))
```

Rules were filtered in four stages:

1. **Apriori** with the support and confidence floors above.
2. **Lift > 1** — discard rules no better than chance.
3. **Redundancy removal** (`is.redundant`) — a rule is redundant when a *more
   general* rule (a subset of its antecedent) achieves at least the same
   confidence. The extra condition earns nothing and only clutters the output.
4. **Statistical significance** — Fisher's exact test on each rule's 2×2
   contingency table, with Benjamini–Hochberg correction for the fact that
   thousands of rules are being tested at once.

`r length(rules)` rules survive all four stages.

## The rule landscape

```{r fig-scatter}
fig("09_rules_scatter")
```

```{r fig-twokey}
fig("10_rules_two_key")
```

The scatter shows the classic trade-off. Rules in the upper-left are rare but
almost deterministic; rules on the right are common but weaker. There is no
single "best" corner — which one matters depends on whether you are designing a
homepage widget (needs support) or a checkout prompt (needs confidence).

## Rules as a network

```{r fig-graph}
fig("11_rules_graph_top25_lift")
```

```{r fig-grouped}
fig("12_rules_grouped_matrix")
```

```{r fig-para}

```

The graph makes the structure obvious: the highest-lift rules are not scattered
across the catalogue, they form **tight clusters within product families** —
the herb marker set, the regency tea set, the woodland/spaceboy children's
range, the jumbo bag colourways. Customers buy *collections*, not individual
objects.

## Sensitivity to the thresholds

```{r fig-sens}
fig("08_threshold_sensitivity")
```

```{r sens-table}
knitr::kable(tab("03_threshold_sensitivity"))
```

Rule count falls roughly geometrically as minimum support rises — the practical
reason support, not confidence, is the parameter to tune first. Confidence
mostly trims an already-determined candidate pool.

# Segment analysis

## UK versus international

```{r seg}
knitr::kable(tab("05_segment_comparison"))
```

```{r seg-rules}
knitr::kable(head(tab("05_top_rules_international"), 10),
             caption = "Top international rules by lift")
```

International baskets are far fewer, so a higher support floor (2%) is needed
to get a comparable rule count. Their association structure is different:
international customers (largely wholesalers) buy in complete product ranges,
which produces very high-lift but narrow rules.

## Seasonal shift

```{r season}
knitr::kable(tab("05_season_comparison"))
```

```{r season-rules}
knitr::kable(head(tab("05_festive_only_rules"), 15),
             caption = "Rules that appear only in the September-November window")
```

The festive quarter yields substantially more rules from *fewer* baskets — gift
buying is more patterned than routine buying. Rules that exist only in this
window are the ones worth building seasonal campaigns around.

# From rules to action

## A rule-based recommender

```{r recsys}
knitr::kable(tab("05_recommender_demo"))
```

Given a partial basket, every rule whose antecedent is fully contained in it
"fires"; the consequents the customer has not already taken, ranked by lift, are
the recommendations. This is a complete cold-start-free recommender that needs
no customer history at all — only the current basket.

## Quantified opportunity

For each rule, the baskets containing the antecedent but *missing* the
consequent are counted directly from support and coverage — no basket scan
needed, since coverage is $\text{supp}(X)$ and support is $\text{supp}(X \cup Y)$:

$$
\text{missed baskets} = \big(\text{coverage} - \text{support}\big) \times N
$$

Multiplying by the rule's confidence and the consequent's average line value
gives an order-of-magnitude estimate of the revenue a well-placed cross-sell
prompt could recover.

```{r value}
knitr::kable(head(tab("05_cross_sell_opportunity_value"), 15))
```

```{r fig-value}
fig("15_cross_sell_opportunity_value")
```

```{r value-total}
val  <- tab("05_cross_sell_opportunity_value")
best <- tab("05_cross_sell_best_rule_per_product")

gbp <- function(x) paste0("GBP ", formatC(round(x), format = "d", big.mark = ","))

knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Basis = c("Naive sum over all rules",
            "Best rule per consequent product",
            "Top 20 products of those",
            "Actual revenue in the period"),
  Estimate = gbp(c(sum(val$PotentialRevenue,  na.rm = TRUE),
                   sum(best$PotentialRevenue, na.rm = TRUE),
                   sum(head(best, 20)$PotentialRevenue, na.rm = TRUE),
                   sum(retail$Revenue))),
  Note = c("Double counts -- upper bound only",
           "Defensible headroom estimate",
           "Where to start",
           "For scale")))
```

Summing across all `r nrow(val)` rules badly double counts: many rules share a
consequent and fire on the same basket. Keeping only the single best rule per
consequent product collapses them to `r nrow(best)` distinct opportunities and
gives the defensible figure — roughly
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * sum(best$PotentialRevenue, na.rm = TRUE) / sum(retail$Revenue))`
of realised revenue in the period.

Note that the biggest opportunities are **not** the highest-lift rules. The herb
marker rules that top the lift table are worth a few hundred pounds each,
because the products are cheap and the sets are already almost always bought
complete. The money is in mid-lift, high-support rules on expensive items —
`ROSES REGENCY TEACUP AND SAUCER ⇒ REGENCY CAKESTAND 3 TIER` has a lift of only
4.6, but it fires on hundreds of baskets and the cakestand is a high-ticket
product. **Lift finds the pattern; support and price decide whether it is worth
acting on.**

---

# Findings and recommendations

**1. Products sell as families, not as individuals.** Nearly every high-lift
rule links members of one product set — herb markers, the regency tea range, the
retrospot lunch bags, the woodland/spaceboy children's line. Lift values of
50–75× are enormous, and mean a customer holding two herb markers is
overwhelmingly likely to be completing the set.

*Action:* sell and merchandise these as bundles. A "complete the set" prompt on
the product page is the single highest-value intervention this analysis
supports, and the rules identify exactly which sets qualify.

**2. Colourway substitution is real and predictable.** Rules link the same
product in different colours (red / pink / blue retrospot bags, white / red
hanging heart holders). Customers buying one variant frequently buy another.

*Action:* show the colour family, not just the SKU, and keep variants in stock
together — a stock-out on one variant depresses sales of the whole cluster.

**3. High confidence without lift is a trap.** Rules ending in
`WHITE HANGING HEART T-LIGHT HOLDER` reach high confidence simply because it
appears in over 12% of all baskets. Lift corrects for this, which is why it was
used as the primary ranking measure throughout.

*Action:* never rank recommendations on confidence alone.

**4. Association structure is seasonal.** Thousands of rules exist only in the
September–November window.

*Action:* re-mine the rules quarterly rather than treating the rule set as
static, and hold separate rule sets for the festive campaign.

**5. Segment the model.** UK and international baskets have measurably different
association structures. A single global rule set serves neither well.

*Action:* maintain per-segment rule sets, at minimum UK versus international.

## Limitations

* **Wholesale contamination.** Very large baskets are wholesale orders, not
  consumer shopping. They inflate co-occurrence counts. A production system
  should mine consumer and wholesale baskets separately.
* **Correlation, not causation.** A rule says two products appear together; it
  does not prove that promoting one *causes* the other to sell. Validation
  requires an A/B test.
* **One year of data.** Trend versus seasonality cannot be separated from a
  single annual cycle.
* **Missing `CustomerID` on ~25% of rows** prevents customer-level basket
  analysis, so this study is purely transaction-level.
* **Support floor hides the long tail.** At 1% support, products selling fewer
  than ~183 baskets a year can never enter a rule, however strong their
  associations are. Niche cross-sells are invisible to this model.

## Possible extensions

* **FP-Growth** (`arules::fim4r` or `rCBA`) for a runtime comparison against
  Apriori on the same data.
* **Sequential pattern mining** (`arulesSequences`, cSPADE) using `CustomerID`
  and `InvoiceDate` to find what customers buy *next*, not just *together*.
* **Product hierarchies** — aggregating SKUs into categories would lift support
  values enough to reveal cross-category rules the SKU-level model misses.
* **Negative association rules** — which products *suppress* each other, useful
  for detecting cannibalisation between variants.
